checkpoint.measure: Score share against fixed practice opponents (0.5 = even)

tiers.label: Practice player = the strongest program (our best)

names: Whole-body hitting at the joint layer

skills.name: Meets the ball near the paddle centre (sees the ball right)
skills.real: Table tennis is among the fastest visuo-motor tasks; two fixed cameras, no ball coordinates. Seen right, the ball meets the paddle centre; a 5 cm perception error loses points.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of own contacts with the ball centre within 5 cm of the paddle centre (hand_center). Scenario recv: the same reading, taken inside the physics step of the contact.

skills.name: Paddle meets the incoming ball (predicting bounce and spin)
skills.real: The ball crosses the net and bounces once on the own half; the bounce and spin have to be predicted for the paddle to be on the ball's path at the right moment.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation points: share of balls landing legally on the own half that the paddle touches (pooled). Scenario recv: the opponent serves every point; share of serves the paddle touches (the scenario record: paddle_A after table_A).

skills.name: Returns the serve onto the table
skills.real: Receiving starts every other point: one chain from seeing the opponent's toss and strike to the own stroke.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of the opponent's legal serves returned onto its half. Scenario recv: the same reading with the opponent serving every point (the scenario record: after paddle_A the next table contact is table_B).

skills.name: Whole-body stroke returns the ball onto the table
skills.real: At the joint layer the paddle face reaches the contact point at the right time, angle and speed, so the ball clears the net and lands.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of incoming balls returned onto the opponent's half (pooled). Scenarios recv + base: the same reading.

skills.name: Stays up when pushed and still plays the ball
skills.real: A stroke is a whole-body action held up by the legs; stable means taking a knock (contact, the stroke's own reaction) and staying up. The legs are entirely the program's; no standing service.
skills.measure: Scenario push: the opponent serves every point; 50 ms after its strike the program's pelvis gets a sideways push (alternating); share of pushed points with no fall. Gate: the program acts and touches ≥ 30 % of the serves in recv (it really plays; a motionless paddle is hit by 3/8 serves).
skills.line: No fall in ≥ 2/3 of the pushed points

skills.name: No fall while playing
skills.real: A fallen robot lies until the point ends.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of matches with ≥ 5 own strokes and no fall. Scenarios base + recv: share of points without a fall.
skills.line: Matches: no fall in 2/3; scenario: ≥ 90 % of points without a fall (gate: touches ≥ 30 % of incoming)

skills.name: Serves legally
skills.real: The ITTF service law: toss, strike on the way down, bounce on the own half, then over the net onto the opponent's.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation: share of own serves that are legal (pooled). Scenario serve: the program serves every point; share of serves judged good (undue delay and a missed toss count as faults).

skills.name: Commands keep pace (real-time timing)
skills.real: A 100 Hz joint layer; commands 3 or more steps late break both strokes and balance.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation / scenarios base + recv, episode command rows: from the first own command to the end, share of steps whose latest own command is at most 3 steps old. Gate: ≥ 5 strokes.

skills.name: Plays rallies
skills.real: Rallies are the body of a match; every stroke has to land for one to go on.
skills.measure: Checkpoint Evaluation / scenario base: share of points with ≥ 3 strokes.

off.name: Placement, reading the opponent, results against the tiers
off.why: Match-result readings (even_middle / even_strongest) stay on the growth curve only.

off.name: Footwork (excluded on the card)
off.why: Every point starts at home, the table is small; excluded on the card.

open_questions: The 30 % 'returns the serve' line: no frozen program passes in the scenario (best Astra final:3 3/16) although Astra touches 15/16. Keep the line, or add a level 'touched and over the net'?
on_time (commands <= 3 steps old) is too sensitive to host load: measure it only in scenarios (fixed host, x3), or drop it from the card?
At 0.8 m/s the reference never falls; raise to 1.2 m/s so push separates programs better (13 more runs, about 30 min)?

notes.challenge: Two humanoids with real paddles and two fixed cameras, no ball coordinates. The program sees the ball, predicts its spin and path and hits with the whole body in real time.

achieved.text: Kimi 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash never won a point on a good serve, each failing differently: Kimi swung at 31 of 33 untouched serves and missed balls 0.50 m away, DeepSeek's missed balls passed 0.95 m away, GLM's arm moved on 0 of 15.
Against the same recorded Opus serve setup Gemini 4 Argon touched 0 of 8 good serves in TTN2-F10 and 8 of 8 in TTN2-F17, won 5 of those points and came back from 0:3 to 11:5.
Serve holding returned at the end: in TTN2-F18 Gemini touched 8 of GPT-6 Astra's 10 serves and won none of those points, and in TTN2-F19 the server won all 29 points.
Claude Opus 5.5 aimed its serve at the receiver: 28 of the points it won on serve ended with the ball hitting the opponent's robot.

GPT-6 Astra: Searched its strokes on the GPU and picked its service side from where the opponent held its paddle; Opus noticed and wrote it down.
GLM 5.3 Flash: Never won a point on its own serve (0 of 42); within one match it fixed a dropped toss, the fix caused delay faults, and the next fix brought the dropped toss back.

interface.sees: Two cameras of its own, behind and beside its robot (480 × 360 each, a new frame every 10 ms), its own joints, balance sensor, position and paddle pose, the sound of hits and bounces, and the score. No ball coordinates.
interface.controls: Targets for all 29 joints: one row, or a plan of up to 300 rows of 10 ms, with optional stiffness and damping; plus a ball toss to serve. Real time, 100 times a second.
interface.moment: Final, GPT-6 Astra v Gemini 4 Argon, match point at 10–7, 1:05 in the replay. Astra's serve has just bounced on Gemini's half and is coming to Gemini's robot (ringed). Gemini's return drops on its own half, and Astra wins 11–7.
details: Cameras: two of the player's own, one behind and above its robot looking down the table, one at the side; 480 × 360 each, 45° vertical field of view, side by side in one image. A new frame every 10 ms; the newest a program can fetch is 20 ms old, stamped with its step.
Not given: where the ball is or how fast it spins. Yellow marks every 0.25 m along the table edges help the program measure what it sees.

Own robot: all 29 joint angles, speeds and torques, the targets and gains in use, the pelvis IMU, the pelvis position, speed and heading from the venue's motion capture, and the paddle's position and face direction.
Referee: point and score, whose serve, the serve's phase and deadline, whether the ball is in play, and the last points with how each was won.
Hearing: the hits, bounces and net touches since the ball was last played, with their times.

Command: targets for all 29 joints (or the 17 of waist and arms), one row or up to 300 rows, one per 10 ms step; optional stiffness and damping and velocity targets. Targets are clipped to the joint ranges and speed limits; the joint controller runs 1000 times a second through the motors' torque–speed curves.
Serve: a toss from behind the end line, 0.16 to 1 m high, struck by the program's own stroke as it falls; it must bounce once on each side.
No ready-made skills: no walking or balance service; the legs belong to the program from the start of every point.
Timing: a control step every 10 ms; the world runs at real speed and never waits; a command acts at the next step, one command in flight.
Rules: ITTF table tennis, one game to 11 with a lead of 2 (or first to 15).
Before the match: 2 hours of preparation with a full practice copy of the table, a practice opponent and a GPU training kit (half an RTX PRO 6000).
